newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Algeria gives green light to tackle internal economy.
newsitem.headline: Algeria gives green light to tackle internal economy.

text.p: Algerian authorities have given the green light to start privatisation across the board in a new phase of an economic revolution quietly transforming the North African country.

Under a privatisation law passed on Sunday, the firms are expected to be put on sale without a requirement for buyers to retain all of the workforce. Officials say they expect about 250 firms to be sold off soon.
It's a delicate issue, after nearly three decades of a jobs-for-life philosophy of a crumbled centralised economy.

The law is a new building block in Algeria's efforts to tackle microeconomic reforms still needed after significant progress in following an IMF prescription for economic recovery, say political and other analysts.
"But it will be a longer process than many would like to think," said one economic specialist in Algiers, seeing three to five years before the future becomes "fairly attractive".
Another commented: "It is advancing at a prudent pace and I would say it will take five, seven or maybe 10 years."

Analysts and diplomats believe Algeria has transformed its macroeconomy since it was forced into debt rescheduling in 1994 and 1995 when interest and principle repayments loomed bigger than export earnings.

Algeria swallowed its pride, agreed to an International Monetary Fund reform programme and rescheduled some $12 billion of its $32 billion foreign debt. It has since followed the reform recipe, by cutting inflation and imports and tightening spending.

"On the macroeconomic front it has done well...This year's budget deficit is very small, debt-service ratio against export earnings will be about 35 percent for the next two years, and they are making progress on inflation," said another analyst.

Hard currency reserves at the end of 1996 were $4 billion, double those of the year before, and the country last week announced a 1996 trade surplus of $4.3 billion against a 1995 deficit of $521 million.
"But microeconomic reforms are far more complex especially in terms of the social and political cost," he added.
"Privatisation has not been moving quickly. Domestic savings for investment are very low, which is not surprising given the decline in the dinar up to 1994, and inflation."

Under its original 1995 privatisation law Algeria has sold about 10 of the 70 firms offered for sale. "The new law should bring a greater spirit of free enterprise, but it is one thing to make a list, it is another thing to sell it," said another analyst.
Algeria is aware of the explosive mix of poverty, unemployment and lack of hope for many of its 29 million people, more than two-thirds of them aged under 30.

Officials have long said these factors drove young people into the ranks of Islamic fundamentalists. They also privately accept the reality put by Western economists that any real switch to a private economy will mean big layoffs.

"Algeria has two economies - the oil and gas of Sonatrach, which is very efficient and very open to foreign involvement, and the rest of the industrial sector which is in a really bad shape," one Western economic specialist said on Monday.

About two million of the five-million-plus workforce are employed in the 400-odd firms in the public sector whose only real success story is in oil and gas -- earning more than 94 percent of foreign currency, or over $12 billion last year.
Overall unemployment is around 30 percent, with about 300,000 new job seekers entering the market each year.

"They will need seven or eight percent growth to absorb the newcomers to the market and maybe a small number of the long-term unemployed. And you will need this growth for several years to bring the jobless rate down to a comfortable level," another economic analyst said on Sunday.
Algeria's gross domestic product (GDP) grew 4.8 percent in 1995 after shrinking 1.8 percent the year before. Officials forecast growth of about five percent for 1996.
Late last month, officials said about 130,000 workers would lose jobs in 1997 and 1998 as the government plans to shut down about 60 units, roughly half of them in the industrial sector.

The non-oil sector is making some progress. The authorities last week said exports outside hydrocarbons earned $881 million last year. Two years ago they earned only around $300 million, despite billions of dollars being pumped in to the sector.

One analyst commented: "I feel a fundamental problem is that some officials still have a strong attachment to an administrative economy. They have put in billion of dollars in the past six years, and some people think more money will still make state enterprises competitive. It will not.
"They need a vision of where they think they will be in five years' time, and need to keep moving to that." -- Rabat newsroom, 212-7-720065
